title: Three-string basses in Italy and the low C extension
summary: His Italian teacher's bass had three strings, as in Bottesini's day; the E string came later, and a lever mechanism extends it to low C for Strauss and Prokofiev.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: When you were a kid, did you see many three-string basses in Italy?

Oh yeah, yeah. In fact, that's all there was. My teacher had a three-string bass in Italy, and that's all there was. In the, in the years of the famous bass player Giovanni Bottezzini, they just had G, D and A, and A was the lowest string in the bass. And it was only recently, I'd say about, ooh, the last 50 years that the E string was added to a bass fiddle.
Wait a second, Rudy. You're talking about three-string basses, famous bass players in Italy.

And how the change has come over to fourth string, huh? Yes. In fact, some fellow in Germany, or even further than that, he invented a machine for the E string, which is the lowest string, and it brings it chromatically down to a C by pushing levers. And a lot of symphony bass players use that. It goes way down to a low C, which is very deep, boom, see, chromatically, you know. Stepwise. E natural, E flat, and way down the line. Half a step at a time, I mean.
Yeah. And what's, what that means.

And of course, that helps tremendously in scores like the way Strauss writes, he writes that, he wants that C a lot of times. And of course, the modern composers like Prokofius, the Cicloish and all those guys, they have written, they want that, those low notes.
